result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers make the same sound choice: system fonts for the app and one self-hosted, subset, open-licence serif at a single weight for marketing headlines, with pasteable CSS. B is more honest about uncertainty. It states its assumptions, hedges on file size and licence, and says to test on a real low-end Android phone and an old laptop. A is tighter and includes a working subsetting command, but it says headings show in Georgia first, which won't happen on Android because Georgia isn't installed there. Neither answer fully explains what Android actually falls back to. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers make the same sound call: system fonts for the app, plus one self-hosted, subset, single-weight open-licence heading font for the marketing site, with tabular figures for payroll numbers. B is easier to paste in, with a working pyftsubset command and a unicode-range. A is more honest about uncertainty: it flags the unmeasured file size, asks the user to confirm the licence, adds a metric-matched fallback idea, and gives concrete testing steps on low-end Android phones and old Windows laptops. A's fallback @font-face is left half-filled, with placeholder comments where the metric overrides should go. Neither answer says that Georgia is usually missing on Android, so headings there will fall back to the device's generic serif.
